w:r.w:t: How a query flows through the app, and what needs fixing in each file.
Written in plain language. Two parts: the query lifecycle map, then the problems and changes per file.
The one thing to take away
The app's whole promise is finding files with meaningless names (like WhatsApp's IMG-WA0023.pdf) by their content.
Right now the indexing pipeline systematically cuts that content out of the AI's understanding — the description is built with the content placed last, and the AI only reads the first ~40-50 words.
So your most important files get understood mostly from boilerplate and a junk filename, with the real content cut off.
The single highest-value fix in the whole codebase: reorder the file description so content comes FIRST. It is nearly free and it directly fixes the core use case.
Part 1 — The life of a query

This is the journey a search takes, from the moment the user speaks or types, to the file appearing on screen. Each box is a stage, names the file that does the work, and shows what goes in and what comes out. Follow the arrows top to bottom.
User speaks or types a search.
Raw query text, e.g. "find my aadhaar card please". Voice is converted to text here first.
A structured query: filler words stripped, category guessed, time/owner/type/share signals detected, a clean version for the AI, and a keyword version for matching.
The structured query + all files held in memory.
Top 50 files scored by how well their filename, folder, and content keywords match. Fast, no AI.
The clean query, turned into a 384-number vector by the AI, compared against a CANDIDATE PILE of files.
Top 50 files scored by meaning. NOTE: the candidate pile is limited — this is where files can be missed.
The two ranked lists from keyword and meaning search.
One combined top-25 list. Keyword matches are currently trusted 3x more than meaning matches.
Final top-10, reordered using meaning similarity, keyword overlap, and several boosts/penalties.
Files on screen. User taps one, opens or shares it.
The indexing side — runs in the background, feeds the search
Search can only find what indexing prepared. This runs once at first launch and incrementally afterwards. It is where the quality of everything above is actually decided.
A prioritised list (Documents, Downloads, WhatsApp first), capped at 5,000 for now, skipping unchanged files.
A text 'description' of the file (category, type, filename, content, date) — THIS is what the AI reads. Content is currently placed LAST.
The description — but only the first ~40-50 words are read.
A 384-number vector representing the file's meaning. Content past ~50 words is cut off.
Saved to the on-phone database, ready for search to pull from.
Indexing (A→D) writes file vectors into the database. Search (stage 3) reads those vectors back to compare against the query.
The SAME AI engine (EmbeddingEngine) is used by both — it turns the query into a vector AND turns each file into a vector, so they live in the same 'meaning space' and can be compared.
The weak link is the join between B and C: the description is built content-last, then C only reads the first part. Fix B's ordering and the whole search improves.
Part 2 — Each file: problems and what to change
In plain language. Files are listed in the order the query touches them. For each: what it does, how serious its issues are, the problems, and the changes to make.
Reads the raw query and pulls out structured signals — category, time, owner, type — and makes a clean version for the AI.
Well-built and matches the right idea: strip the filler, keep the meaning. The issues are precision bugs, not structural.
It treats "2024, 2025, 2026" as 'this year' by literally listing the years. This rots — in 2027 it will be wrong, and it gets worse every January.
It checks if a word is 'contained' in the query, so "id" matches inside "video", "bridge", "hidden". This causes wrong category guesses.
The name logic blocks a tiny list of North-Indian surnames (Kumar, Singh, Sharma...). It misfires for the thousands of names not on the list.
Compute the current year dynamically instead of hardcoding years.
Match whole words, not substrings — tokenize the query into words once and check membership.
Treat the surname list as a known limitation; revisit with real data later. Not urgent.
Lowercase the query once and reuse it, instead of re-lowercasing in every function.
Handles many languages and scripts — strips stop words, converts Romanized Hindi (dhundo→find), bridges scripts, and computes a language ranking multiplier.

The most ambitious file, and the riskiest. It supports ~20 languages for an app whose users are Hindi/English in India — lots of untested surface area — and it contains a multiplier that can make correct files vanish.

If a file's name matches the detected language it is boosted 6x; if not, it is multiplied by 0.08 — basically deleted. If language detection misfires (and it can), the correct file silently disappears from results.
~20 languages are supported but only Hindi and English are actually used. Every other language is untested risk, collisions, and maintenance with zero benefit today.
Short words like 'me' / 'mi' / 'mein' mean different things in different languages but are crammed into flat maps, so behaviour is unpredictable for mixed/short inputs.
Same substring problem as elsewhere, and the alias expansion runs a nested loop over the whole alias map for every token — and this runs during indexing for every file.
Tame the language multiplier: gentle down-weight (like 0.7x) for a mismatch, not 0.08x. A wrong guess should cost a few ranks, never make a file vanish.
Cut scope to Hindi and English for now. Add languages back when you actually enter those markets. Huge simplification, zero real loss.
Fix substring matching to whole-word, and precompute the alias lookup so indexing isn't doing nested-loop string work per file.
The conductor of search. Runs the keyword branch and the meaning branch, fuses them, and sends the top candidates to the reranker.
Clean, well-structured orchestration — genuinely good. But it contains the most important non-obvious issue in the codebase: the meaning-search is starved of the files it needs to do its job.
For a vague query with no category, the meaning-search only looks at the first 800 files in storage order — not the best 800. A file at position 2,400 is never even considered.

For detailed queries, the candidate pile is ONLY the files keyword-search already found. So meaning-search can't rescue a badly-named file that keyword-search missed — which is the entire reason it exists.
In the fusion, keyword matches get 3x weight. For your users with junk-named WhatsApp files, that leans hardest on the weakest signal for your most important files.
One spot assumes a list isn't empty and would crash if it were; another spot guards against it. A small landmine if the guard ever changes.
Make the candidate pile category-aware even for specific queries, so meaning-search can reach badly-named files in the right category — not just re-rank keyword hits.
Replace the arbitrary 'first 800' with a smarter selection (by category and recency).
Re-test the 3x keyword weight on real Indian phones — it may need to be lower (or favour meaning) for junk-named files.
Make the two fallbacks consistent so neither can crash.
Instrument this file heavily: log whether the clicked file was even in the candidate pile. This is where recall is won or lost.
The keyword scorer. Scores every file by how well filename, folder, content, and metadata match the query words.
Fast and reasonable, but it carries the same silent-burial pattern: several aggressive multipliers stack with no floor, so a small detection error can delete a good file from results.
If the query is guessed to be about photos and a file is a document, the score is multiplied by 0.05 — basically deleted. If the type guess is wrong, your document vanishes.
It applies the dangerous 6x/0.08x language multiplier from MultilingualBridge right here in scoring, so the same vanishing risk lands on the score.
Six multipliers chain together. Two misfiring low (0.08 × 0.05) annihilate even a strong keyword match. Correctness depends on every detector being right.
A filename match scores 100, a content match only 25. So a well-named irrelevant file outranks a badly-named relevant one — the opposite of what your users need.
Put a floor under the combined multiplier so a strong match can never be reduced below a visible minimum.
Soften the 0.05 type penalty and 0.08 language penalty to gentle down-weights.
Reconsider content-vs-filename weighting for junk-named files (raise content's weight) — tune with real data.
The AI engine. Turns text (query or file description) into a 384-number vector, and compares vectors. The only file that touches the model.
Low severity (but holds the big decision)

The cleanest, best-written file — strong systems work. Keeps the model warm to avoid heat, manages threads for thermal load, cleans up memory properly. The issues are subtle; the big item is a decision, not a bug.
When indexing, it cuts each file's description to ~64 tokens before the AI reads it. Combined with FileMetadata putting content last, the real content gets cut off — this is the core problem.
It only works if vectors are already normalised (they are today). A future caller passing a raw vector gets a silently wrong number, no error.
If a description ends up empty, it silently produces a junk vector instead of skipping the file.
No shrinking applied. This is why the app isn't downloadable for real users yet. Not a bug — the open decision.
Raise the indexing word limit so more content reaches the AI (balance against speed/heat).
Add a safety check or clear label to the similarity function so it can't be silently misused.
Skip or flag files with no real content instead of embedding emptiness.

BIG ONE: quantize the model to INT8 (~390MB → ~100MB). This makes it downloadable AND faster AND cooler — all at once. Then test Hindi quality. If it holds, your biggest blocker is solved. Swapping the model is a clean, contained change here.
The conductor of indexing. Walks the phone, decides what to index, batches files through the AI, and saves them.
Clean, incremental, defensive (batch fails → retries one by one), hardware-aware. Solid work. The issues are about scale and a redundant pass.
Files past 5,000 (by priority) are never indexed and the user is never told. They search for a real file, find nothing, assume the app is broken. The silence is the danger, not the number.
The cap exists partly because every file is held in RAM and scanned per keystroke. Raising it isn't just a number change — it stresses memory and typing speed on cheap phones.
After indexing it does a second full pass that reloads everything and re-runs the slow alias expansion. Wasteful on large libraries.
Benchmarks are estimates; content extraction (slow disk reads per PDF) likely makes real first-index slower than claimed.
Whatever the cap, tell the user when they exceed it and what is/isn't indexed. Never silently truncate.
Find the real ceiling by testing on a real Redmi; set the cap from device memory, not a fixed number.
Fold the keyword backfill into the main pass; don't do a second full pass.
Add incremental search unlocking — let users search priority folders within a minute while the rest finishes in the background.
Only do the bigger 'don't hold everything in RAM' rebuild once real users prove they need larger libraries.
Builds the text 'description' of each file that the AI reads, plus assigns categories. The most important file for search quality.
This is where the core problem lives. Everything search does depends on the description this file builds — and it builds it in the wrong order for the AI's word limit.

The description reads 'A [category] [type] named [filename] containing [content]...'. The content — the only good signal for junk-named files — comes after the boilerplate, exactly where the AI's ~50-word cut removes it.

Well-named files survive (their name is early and meaningful). Junk-named WhatsApp files don't — their useless name is early, their real content is late and gets cut. The files you most need to find are the ones hurt most.
Same substring bug — 'id' matches inside many words, causing wrong categories that then feed the recall problems downstream.
Every PDF nudged to two categories —
Each PDF is pushed toward both Education and Identity regardless of content — a coarse guess for a country where PDFs are bills, statements, forms, everything.
Each PDF is opened and read several times while building metadata — the slowest part of indexing, with redundancy.
THE key change: reorder the description so content and meaningful tokens come FIRST, boilerplate last. Nearly free, biggest impact in the codebase. Directly fixes the junk-named-file problem.
Extract each file's content once and reuse it (don't re-read the PDF multiple times).
Refine the per-PDF category guess once you have real query data.
Storage layer, content extraction, and the final reranking stage. (Reviewed at a lighter depth.)

Not yet deep-dived line by line, but flagged from the architecture: the reranker is the most heuristic, most guessed-constant file and likely repeats the aggressive-multiplier pattern; ContentExtractor's scanned-PDF gap (no text layer) means many junk-named image-PDFs get no content at all; DatabaseHelper stores vectors as blobs and loads candidates — fine at small scale, the FTS-vs-vector decision lives here.
Expect the same silent-burial multiplier pattern in the final ordering — worth the same floor/soften fixes.
Scanned PDFs and photos have no text layer, so content extraction returns nothing — and those are exactly the junk-named files. OCR is deferred to V2.
In-memory candidate loading is fine now; a true on-disk vector index is the path if libraries grow large.
Read GraniteReranker next with the floor/soften lens.
Accept the scanned-PDF gap for V1; plan OCR for V2 driven by real 'couldn't find' data.
Leave the storage design until users prove they need larger scale.
Across all files, here is what to fix and in what order — ranked by impact on whether a user actually finds their file, which is the only thing that matters.
Fix before any user touches the app
1. Reorder the file description (FileMetadata) so content comes first — fixes the core junk-named-file problem.
2. Tame the silent-burial multipliers (MultilingualBridge + LexicalSearch) — add a floor so correct files can't vanish.
3. Quantize the model to INT8 (EmbeddingEngine) — makes the app downloadable, faster, and cooler. Then test Hindi.
4. Widen the meaning-search candidate pile (SearchPipeline) so it can reach badly-named files, not just re-rank keyword hits.
5. Make the 5,000 cap honest (FileIndexer) — tell users what is and isn't indexed.
6. Switch substring matching to whole-word everywhere (QueryEnricher, MultilingualBridge, LexicalSearch, FileMetadata).
7. Cut multilingual scope to Hindi + English until you enter other markets.
8. Re-tune the keyword-vs-meaning weight on real phones.
9. Read GraniteReranker, DatabaseHelper, ContentExtractor in depth.
10. Consider the on-disk index only when users prove they need larger libraries.

The encouraging part: none of the top fixes is a rewrite. Reordering one sentence, softening some multipliers, and swapping in a smaller model are all surgical changes. Together they move Ru from an impressive demo that struggles on real phones to something that actually finds the file.
